blogs.title: When the Patient 'Forgets to Breathe': Chiari I as Acquired Central Hypoventilation
blogs.description: This post would explore how Chiari I can compress medullary respiratory centers, preserving voluntary breathing while impairing automatic ventilation during sleep or distraction. It would focus on the clinical clue of profound desaturation without dyspnea and discuss when unexplained hypoxemia and central apneas should prompt brain and craniocervical imaging rather than more pulmonary testing.

blogs.title: Choking on Normal Scopes: Neurogenic Dysphagia in Chiari I
blogs.description: This post would use the case to revisit dysphagia that affects solids and liquids equally, especially after repeatedly normal laryngoscopy and endoscopy. It would review lower cranial nerve involvement in Chiari, the role of videofluoroscopic swallow studies, and when persistent choking should trigger a neurological rather than purely GI or ENT workup.

blogs.title: When a 'Mild' Sleep Study Isn't Mild: The Type III PSG Trap
blogs.description: This post would examine why an AHI of 6 can be falsely reassuring in suspected central hypoventilation, particularly when most events are central and the study lacks EEG. It would discuss total recording time versus true sleep time, why type III studies can underestimate severity, and how capnography and full polysomnography fit into evaluating brainstem-related sleep-disordered breathing.

blogs.title: The Old CT That Wasn't Normal: Diagnostic Delay and the Crowded Foramen Magnum
blogs.description: This post would focus on the 14-year delay created by a missed radiologic clue on an earlier head CT. It would discuss anchoring, specialty siloing, and the value of re-reviewing prior imaging in patients with persistent unexplained symptoms, while also highlighting practical CT findings that should raise suspicion for Chiari I.

blogs.title: Chiari I Is Not a Number: Incidental Tonsillar Ectopia vs Symptomatic Chiari Syndrome
blogs.description: This post would address the modern tension between common MRI-detected tonsillar descent and truly symptomatic Chiari disease. It would argue that millimeters alone do not determine significance, reviewing how symptom pattern, brainstem dysfunction, CSF crowding, and functional impact should drive referral and decompression decisions.

blogs.title: Did Trauma Cause It or Unmask It? Post-Traumatic Chiari Phenotypes
blogs.description: This post would analyze the uncertain relationship between minor trauma and later Chiari symptoms, asking whether injury can create secondary tonsillar descent or simply reveal a previously silent malformation. It would also examine how post-traumatic headache syndromes and atypical scalp allodynia can misdirect clinicians away from a structural posterior fossa diagnosis.
